doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Love of doo wop and gospel and adding voices on records
summary: Dorn says doo wop and gospel shaped his production. He used Cissy Houston and the Sweet Inspirations for backing voices and explains how he builds vocal parts in the studio.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. I think he’s since re-recorded it more recently.
So going from artist to artist, how much of your love of early rock & roll influenced —

I guess, you know like I really love rock & roll, real rock & roll, and I really love what people call doo wop, the groups. My two favorite musics probably are doo wop and Gospel. And so when you love something you have a certain sensibility like I like to put strings and voices on and horns on a lot of the jazz records I made, the commercial ones, but the voices were always Cissy Houston and the Sweet Inspirations, because of work they had done with Aretha and because they were all out of the church. Cissy ran a choir in a church in Newark. And I can ask certain people for specific things, you know? I mean I went on to make some doo wop things, I made like a semi-classic doo wop record with a guy named Kenny Vance called “Looking for an Echo,” which kind of became an anthem for the oldies crowd. And I worked with Dion once or twice, we did some things and he’s like one of my favorite artists in the universe you know. But I think it’s the love of music in general and if any of the like Gospel or rock & roll or those things, if any of those elements came in it was in ways I would approach things, especially in how I would color stuff. You know like I really enjoy doing voices, adding voices, layering voices and doing all kinds of tricks with background vocals and hiding them inside of strings and doing that kind of stuff.
And how did that happen in the studio? You invite these singers in? Is there a vocal arranger who works?

Anybody that I brought in or anybody that I bring in now, you know, once we get that first layer, whether it’s voice and piano, voice and rhythm, saxophone, whatever it is — the basic layer where the record’s complete, now if you add stuff it’ll work or not work based on whether if it works or not works. The only time I use arrangers would be for specific things, like strings, sometimes horns. But voices, even with horns sometimes I’ll get like three or four guys and we’ll just say like all right, what goes here? Give me some Al Green. Give me some Memphis, give me some New Orleans. And we figure it out on the spot. But the voices — I got a new girl I just signed to Rykodisc, it’s like a twenty- first century Carole King, and she’s young, she’s in her twenties, but she has a sixties, seventies sensibility as a songwriter and a singer. So it’ll give me a chance to make modern versions of that classic form. So we’ve been making demos, and I’m able to do some of my old tricks again. Because there’s a young person that comes from that time. She is now, but she’s from that. So that’s a lot of fun, man.
